About this lexicon

Macrons, usage and evidence

Macrons mark long vowels; short vowels are left plain. A heavy syllable is not automatically a long vowel. Consonantal i is written j (jam, ejus, conjungō), and the vowel before intervocalic j is left unmarked (major); search treats i and j alike. Inflected examples, genitives, principal parts and Latin headings are included in the review.

For ancient vocabulary, the main references are Lewis & Short and Lewis’s Elementary Latin Dictionary through Perseus and Logeion, with Dickinson’s core list for cross-checking. Hidden quantities are also compared against Bennett’s discussion with Michelson’s corrections and notes on Allen. Dictionary omissions are not automatically proof of shortness; disputed lengths are identified where relevant.

The lexicon is English–Latin. Another language is cited only where it helps to explain a Latin word, its meaning or its form.

For modern words, the classical lengths of inherited roots and regular Latin endings are retained where justified. Loanword stem quantities that the checked sources do not establish are explicitly labelled. “Reading convention” marks an adopted reconstruction, rather than an attested ancient pronunciation.

Ancient Latin means the word and its relevant basic sense are ancient. Lexicographic evidence means a modern dictionary records the expression; it does not imply universal acceptance. Modern extension applies an older word to a modern object. Working formation identifies our own phrase or name adaptation.

Example sentences are composed for everyday conversation, many of them with a small child. They are not quotations unless an author and passage are identified. Noun genitives and genders, important sense distinctions, and known alternative forms are supplied where useful.

Every entry has a page of its own. Each Latin form is labelled with its period, and numbered notes give the reason wherever we depart from Lewis & Short or a source. Each Latin word that heads a term has a page too, which lists every entry that uses it. Our rulings on disputed words are kept, with their evidence and history, on the rulings page; the rules behind them are on How we decide.

Review notes · 8 November 2026

All 53 original grouped entries were reviewed; 39 household and family entries were added. Quantities, examples, definitions and attestation labels were checked separately. The review also removes unsupported precise dates, unsourced principal parts and blanket “attested” tags.

5 October 2026 addition: three family-play entries cover trampoline jumping, Sīmius et arbor and Nauta et undae. The game titles and spoken prompts are our own; modern senses are labelled. The plural genua has short u.

7 October 2026 addition: ausum is the preferred ancient word for “adventure” in the sense of a daring undertaking or venture; adventūra is retained as a medieval/modern alternative, with its semantic development explicitly noted.

11 October 2026 addition: seven workshop-and-repair entries distinguish ancient tool vocabulary from later technical Latin and our own descriptive formations. The review replaces the earlier unsupported cochleārius for “screwdriver” with lexicographically attested vertitōrium, prefers forceps for pliers, records variable vowel quantity in cochlea and terebra, and distinguishes a “dowel” (scalmus) from a wall plug. For the latter, ancora mūrālis plastica is explicitly marked as our provisional descriptive formation, not as an attested traditional term.

18 October 2026 addition: 27 grouped entries cover the family smoothie guide: ingredients, equipment, materials, measurements, preparation verbs and phrases for cooking with a child. Traupman’s uploaded Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, Morgan–Owens and ancient dictionaries were compared. Recorded modern terms, older words with modern senses, uncertain quantities and our composed descriptions are labelled separately. Start with smoothie ingredients · Source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover construction, house layout, furnishings, trowels, a crowbar, extension leads, cable reels and sheet-metal shears. Existing workshop entries were extended with the recorded tape-measure phrase. Descriptive formations and uncertain ancient senses remain explicit. Construction vocabulary source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover hooks, swinging, pipes, gravel, movement, flips, trenches, dirt, heaps, squeezing/crushing, crashes, missions/quests, caps, scaffolding and its parts/actions. Eight existing entries were extended or cross-linked for rods/bars, blankets, lids, planks, wiping and food-preparation verbs. This batch adds English–Latin vocabulary only. Physical senses, modern applications and our composed descriptions remain distinct. Site and play vocabulary source audit.

25 October 2026: a dedicated Lūdī et lūdibria category adds 14 grouped playground/toy entries and brings the existing swing entry into the same filter. Playground source audit.

26 October 2026: classical sources and corrections for the site and construction vocabulary. Two entries are added: the adze, ascia, and ground level, basement, terrace, wing and extension. Scaffolding now leads with māchina and Vitruvius’s arrēctāria / trānsversāria; norma is written without a macron; coctilis has a short i. tabula spūmea is our working formation for EPS board. Site vocabulary corrections.

29 October 2026: the sitting room is exedra (Vitruvius, Cicero; Traupman p. 125), not sessōrium, whose ancient senses are “seat” and, in one passage of Petronius, “dwelling”; concrete is opus caementīcium, after Vitruvius’s caementīcius, not Traupman’s concrētum; jentāculum and jentō have a short e, as Lewis & Short leaves them.

29 October 2026 addition: the daily-life vocabulary of the seven fābulae Theodōrus et pater (I Iter in Lūsitāniam to VII Diēs ūnus Osoitsae), first proposed on 23 October and rebased on the revised texts: 75 grouped entries (entry-196 to entry-270) cover travel, town and shops, place names, weather and landscape, trees, animals, market food, kitchen work, the house and its rebuilding, and phrases for the day. A new category, Urbs, vīcus et loca, holds town, shop and place-name vocabulary. Where a proposed card duplicated an existing one (body parts, vegetables, playground, slide, swing, sandpit, ball games, balance bike, rooms, builders, building timber, family, and the adze card of 26 October), its new words and examples were added to that card instead. Every example marked “Fābula” was re-quoted from the texts as revised on 29 October, in their j orthography. The fork is furcilla (not fuscinula), and mantēle leads with its classical sense, the hand towel. Corrections made on 23 October: jentāculum (short e), būtȳrum, pōtiō, lac, lacūna, īnstrūmentum, vēsīca īnflāta and ēlectricus; alternatives were added to the coffee, tram, trampoline, stick, back, balloon, wake-up, hug, pepper, pumpkin, cutting-board, peel and berry entries. Search libelli to see the addition.

29 October 2026 addition: the everyday words worked into the fābulae in the 29 October vocabulary pass, with an everyday-vocabulary survey of the texts. 14 grouped entries (entry-271 to entry-284) cover electric light and sockets, kitchen appliances, the bathroom, the car, getting about, Dad’s bag, fine weather, geography, time, exclamations and spoken phrases, quiet and gestures, and cooking words from the Culīna Theodōrī; 42 existing entries gain words and examples (family, sleep, bed, clothes, towels, teeth, body, feelings, rooms, cupboards, stairs, doors and shutters, ball games, birds, shops, the table). Every example is quoted from the current texts; Traupman pages were checked in the book. The bath towel is linteum and the hand towel mantēle (not gausapina or manutergium); trulla is also the ladle; the toothbrush is pēniculus dentārius beside pēnicillus; lābellum has a long ā (de Vaan). Search vocabulary to see the addition.

7 November 2026: the Theodōrus et pater readers are cited as Libellī I–VII (Ad Larem avītum), the name on their covers, not as fābulae, which now means only the tales told inside them; their entries’ anchors change accordingly (#fabulae-265 is now #libelli-265). All of the roughly 400 examples quoted from the libellī were checked again against the texts as they stand on 7 November, and 76 that later revisions had changed were re-quoted or replaced. Pyjamas are vestis nocturna, the household word; Traupman’s synthesis dormītōria is noted but not used. The high chair, which has left the texts, is dropped from the furniture entry. Dad’s hip bag is sacculus scorteus; the tablecloth in the libellī is linteum; the heel of a shoe is fulmenta (Plautus), beside Traupman’s fulmentum. Search libelli to see the entries.

8 November 2026: the lexicon is now English–Latin throughout; the Bulgarian glosses, labels and search terms were removed.

8 November 2026: the first 23 words move to the new record format, one record per concept with its own page: hiccups, burping and tickling; “perhaps”; twelve swimming words; seven pots and kitchen utensils. Their notes give the evidence for lutra, caccabus and fortasse against Lewis & Short, and the rulings behind them are collected on the rulings page. The conversation category is now Sermō cotīdiānus: personal names belong in example sentences, not in categories or tags. pōculum ānsātum now has its long a, like olla ānsāta.

Selected quantity corrections
  • ramus / ramulus / ramos → rāmus / rāmulus / rāmōs
  • gravedō / gravedinis → gravēdō / gravēdinis
  • involucrum / manubrium → involūcrum / manūbrium
  • scabī / vesīca / semita → scābī / vēsīca / sēmita
  • vaccinium / morum → vaccīnium / mōrum
  • frīgeō / algēō / fervēō / languēō → frīgeō / algeō / ferveō / langueō
  • elaborātiō / recognitiō → ēlabōrātiō / recōgnitiō
  • program(m)ātum as a noun genitive plural → programmatum; verbal programmātum is a different form
Usage corrections

Ancient fermentō, fermentēscō and vapōrō are no longer called exclusively later inventions. Berry names distinguish modern botanical use from uncertain ancient identification. Totoro, the magnetic-toy phrase and specific Git phrases are labelled as our own adaptations.

The kettle expression and unsupported yogurt or coffee stem quantities are described with their actual level of evidence. Source links appear inside each entry.
